text: explain shortly to me how the property tests work and what they test

items.html:
Property tests don't check one hand-picked input against one stored answer. They generate many random inputs within bounded ranges and check a law that must hold for every one of them. When a case fails, the framework shrinks it to the simplest failing input and saves it, so it's replayed on every later run.

How they run

  • Rust: proptest! blocks in crates/treams-core/src/properties/*.rs and in inline test modules. Strategies generate things like degrees and orders, lossy wavenumbers, lattices and splits. Failing seeds are saved in proptest-regressions/.
  • Python: Hypothesis @given tests in tests/, with strategies such as random materials, sphere clusters or basis layouts. Budgets are 30 examples locally, 100 in CI (with fixed seeds, so CI runs are reproducible) and 300 in a "thorough" profile.
  • Tolerances come from the expected rounding error (a few ulps of the relevant magnitude), not from whatever happened to pass.

What they test

  • Gradients are exact: each analytic gradient must pair correctly with its forward computation, matching finite differences or a dot-product test. Scaling identities such as Euler's relation (scaling positions and wavenumbers together) must hold for the gradients too.
  • Physics:
    • Reciprocity, so T-matrices have the right symmetry.
    • Energy conservation: lossless S-matrices are unitary, and scattering equals extinction for lossless particles.
    • Maxwell scaling: shrinking the wavenumber and growing the particle by the same factor leaves the T-matrix unchanged.
    • Power balance in periodic arrays.
  • Algebra:
    • Rotations compose and invert correctly, and translations obey the addition theorem.
    • Wigner D matrices are unitary.
    • Bessel functions satisfy their Wronskian and recurrence identities.
  • Choices that must not matter:
    • Helicity and parity bases give the same observables.
    • Lattice sums don't depend on the Ewald split, the chosen lattice basis, or which cell the Bloch vector is in.
    • Sums are continuous as a point approaches the lattice plane or axis.
    • Array layouts and strides (reversed, broadcast, read-only) give identical results.
  • Agreement with independent references:
    • Direct lattice sums, where they converge absolutely.
    • Spectral against Ewald evaluation where both apply.
    • High-precision mpmath tables, and upstream treams.

The current cut keeps all of these laws. It removes duplicates: the same identity copied per family, or pinned single-input tests that a property already covers.

text: original treams had these weird numpy to python parsing functions that were named like dddddd does that still exist?

items.html:
Not as something you interact with. Those dddddd names are NumPy ufunc type signatures, not parsing functions: d is float64, D is complex128 and l is int64. llllll->d means "six integer inputs, one float output". In upstream treams the public functions are ufuncs, generated per signature by Cython, so you see them directly: treams.special.wigner3j.types is ['llllll->d'], and incgamma.types is ['dd->d', 'dD->D'].

In treams-rs they only survive inside the native extension:

  • There is one registration table in crates/treams-py/src/ufunc.rs, with entries like (c"jv", &["dD->D"], &[bessel_loop::<…>]). It tells NumPy which input/output types each compiled loop accepts, so NumPy handles broadcasting, casting, strides and out= for us.
  • Behind that table sits one generic strided loop driver, from round 1, not a separately generated function per type combination.
  • The public functions (treams_rs.special.wigner3j, incgamma, …) are ordinary Python functions that call these hidden ufuncs, so users never see type strings; treams_rs.special.wigner3j.types doesn't exist.
  • You'll also see the strings as labels in test and check output, for example wigner3j[dddddd->d] in the floating-point-mode check, because that check runs every registered loop.

They can't go away entirely while we use NumPy ufuncs, because that's how NumPy picks the compiled loop. What could be trimmed is the number of registered variants, for example dropping separate real-only loops and letting NumPy cast to complex. That changes speed and precision for real inputs, though, so I'd leave it unless you want it.

text: right i guess i’m just wondering whether in the treams-rs version this is cleaner and more maintainable or not

items.html:
It's cleaner, with one leftover weak spot.

What's cleaner than upstream treams

  • One pattern per function. treams builds each ufunc by hand in Cython: a loop function per type combination, arrays of function pointers, type codes and data pointers, and a PyUFunc_FromFuncAndData call. That's spread over about eight compiled modules plus declaration files, so adding a function touches several places. In treams-rs each function is written the same way:
    • The kernel is ordinary safe Rust, such as special::bessel(...).
    • A small scalar_loop! block of about 5 lines turns it into a NumPy loop.
    • One row in the registration table gives its name, type signature and loop.
  • Unsafe code in one place. The pointer and stride handling, including negative and zero strides, lives in one shared driver. So do the floating-point guard, the parallel threshold and error reporting. The loops themselves contain no unsafe code.
  • Type strings are internal. Users call normal Python functions with docstrings and type stubs; the ufuncs behind them are hidden.

What isn't clean yet

  • The type strings are hand-written and must match the Rust argument types by convention. A row like &["dD->D"] has to agree with (order: f64, z: Complex). The macro's comment says so, but if they disagree the loop reads memory as the wrong type. That is undefined behaviour, and only tests would catch it. The fix is to derive the signature from the Rust types at compile time (f64 → d, Complex → D, integer → l). That removes the hand-written strings and the hazard.
  • Magic numbers in the generics. Entries like bessel_loop::<2, false, 1> mean "Hankel H1, not spherical, first derivative"; named constants or enums would read better.
  • ufunc.rs is still large: 1,975 lines, against 1,899 on the original main.

So it's structurally better than treams, but not yet as maintainable as it could be. Deriving the signatures from the types and naming the kind parameters would be a natural addition to the core lane's cut. I can queue it for right after that lane merges.
